HW 9: Varying intercepts and partial pooling

Due: Thursday, Apr 1 at 2:30 pm on Canvas · Size: full analysis · Points: 25 · Covers: Multilevel models 1

Start from the homework template, use ## Q1 to ## Q6 headings, and turn in both the .qmd and the rendered .html. Save brms fits with file =.

Data. If you have your own nested data (repeated measures within people, people within groups), you may use it: say what the levels are. Otherwise use this version of the classic sleep-deprivation study: reaction times (ms) for 18 people across days of sleep restriction. To make partial pooling visible, some people “missed sessions,” so people have between 3 and 10 observations.

library(tidyverse)
data(sleepstudy, package = "lme4")   # install.packages("lme4") if needed

set.seed(9)
keep <- tibble(Subject = unique(sleepstudy$Subject),
               n_days = sample(c(2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 10, 10), 18, replace = TRUE))
sleep <- sleepstudy |>
  left_join(keep, by = "Subject") |>
  mutate(u = runif(n())) |>
  group_by(Subject) |>
  filter(rank(u) <= n_days) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(Reaction, Days, Subject)

Q1. The structure (3 points)

  1. How many people, how many observations in total, and how many per person (range)?
  2. Plot each person’s raw mean reaction time against how many observations they have. Which people’s means would you trust least, and why?

Q2. The empty model (4 points)

  1. Write the varying-intercept model Reaction ~ 1 + (1 | Subject) in likelihood notation, with all levels: the observation-level likelihood, the distribution of person intercepts, and priors (including for the between-person SD).
  2. Fit it. Interpret the intercept, the between-person SD (sd(Intercept)), and σ, in milliseconds.
  3. Compute the intraclass correlation (ICC = between-person variance / total variance) draw by draw and report it with a 95% interval. What does it mean for these data?

Q3. Complete, no, and partial pooling (5 points)

  1. Fit (or compute) three estimates of each person’s mean reaction time:
    • complete pooling: one mean for everyone (Reaction ~ 1);
    • no pooling: each person on their own (Reaction ~ 0 + Subject, or just the raw means);
    • partial pooling: each person’s intercept from your Q2 model (e.g., add_epred_draws() per person, or coef()).
  2. Make a table or quick plot comparing the no-pooling and partial-pooling estimates for each person. Who moved the most toward the grand mean, and why them? Use both their number of observations and how far their raw mean was from the grand mean in your answer.
  3. In two or three sentences: why is partial pooling usually a better bet for predicting a person’s next observation than either extreme?

Q4. Add a level-1 predictor (4 points)

  1. Fit Reaction ~ 1 + Days + (1 | Subject). Write it in likelihood notation.
  2. Interpret the Days coefficient.
  3. Compare sd(Intercept) and σ with the empty model. Why did they change? (Hint: think about which days each person happened to be observed on.)

Q5. Predicting a known person vs. a new person (4 points)

Using your Q4 model, predict reaction time at Day 5:

  1. for Subject 308 (an existing person; use the default re_formula = NULL), and
  2. for a new person not in the data (re_formula = NULL, allow_new_levels = TRUE with a new Subject value, or sample_new_levels = "gaussian").

Report the expected value (epred) for each with a 95% interval. Why is the new person’s interval so much wider? Which piece of the model does that extra width come from?

Q6. Publication-ready shrinkage figure (5 points)

Make a figure that meets the checklist showing partial pooling in action for the empty model:

  • each person’s no-pooling estimate (raw mean) and partial-pooling estimate, connected (e.g., arrows from raw to pooled) so the shrinkage is visible;
  • the grand mean as a reference line;
  • the number of observations per person shown somehow (point size, labels, or sorting), so a reader can see that people with fewer observations shrink more;
  • labels in words and units, a stand-alone caption, ggsave() at 6.5 inches wide, and the one or two sentences you’d put in a paper to explain it.
TipUnder the hood: how brms builds the person effects (optional, not graded)

Run stancode() on your Q2 model and find these lines:

array[M_1] vector[N_1] z_1;            // in parameters
r_1_1 = (sd_1[1] * (z_1[1]));          // in transformed parameters
target += std_normal_lpdf(z_1[1]);     // in model

brms doesn’t sample each person’s deviation r directly. It samples a standardized version z ~ Normal(0, 1) and multiplies by the between-person SD: r = τ × z. This is called the non-centered parameterization.

  1. Mathematically, why is r = τ × z with z ~ Normal(0, 1) the same as r ~ Normal(0, τ)?
  2. Why might it sample better? (Think back to HW 5: when τ is near 0, all the r’s are squeezed near 0, and the posterior gets a narrow “funnel” shape that is hard for HMC to explore. Does z have that problem?)

Nothing to turn in. If you’re curious, SR 13.4 covers this in detail.
